newsitem.title: UK: UK sources hopeful of Eurofighter deal.
newsitem.headline: UK sources hopeful of Eurofighter deal.

text.p: Britain is hopeful Germany can overcome the problems which have hampered development of the four-country Eurofighter, a project which holds the key to thousands of British jobs, defence sources said on Tuesday.

British Defence Secretary George Robertson is due to meet his counterpart Volker Ruehe in Germany on Wednesday ahead of talks on Friday between Prime Minister Tony Blair and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
Media reports have speculated that a deal could be struck in time for the Blair-Kohl talks. The sources said on Tuesday they hoped a statement will be issued after Robertson meets Ruehe.

Ruehe said on Sunday he was confident that Bonn, under pressure to tighten budgets and qualify for European monetary union, would find the funds needed to buy 180 Eurofighter jets to replace its ageing Phantom jets and modernise its air force.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel has proposed redirecting state aid for the Airbus airliner to the four-nation Eurofighter project to help toward the planned 23 billion mark purchase.
Ruehe has already offered to provide a billion marks from his own budget and if Waigel comes up with another billion, production of the jet can start.
Eurofighter, developed jointly by Germany, Britain, Italy and Spain, is designed to be the next generation of fighter jet.
But Britain has warned that the dispute between Germany's defence and finance ministries over whether to go ahead with the purchase is increasing doubts about Eurofighter's viability.
In particular, delays to the project could hit export hopes at a time when both the United Arab Emirates and Norway have shortlisted Eurofighter for their air forces.
Robertson told parliament in a written answer on Monday that Eurofighter already sustained 6,000 jobs in Britain -- a figure which was expected to rise to 14,000 at the peak of production.
The media reports suggested Britain will encourage Germany to go ahead with Eurofighter by signing up to the European Future Large Aircraft (FLA) programme.
The FLA is designed to provide a home grown European alternative to the C130J Hercules produced by Lockheed Martin of the United States.
Robertson said in another answer on Monday the FLA was "a potential solution to our future air transport requirements".

The FLA is being developed by Airbus Industrie, a consortium made up of French state-owned Ste Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7768
